title: Born in Bethlehem, Presented in the Temple
summary: A census decreed by Caesar Augustus brings Joseph and the pregnant Mary to Bethlehem, where Jesus is born and laid in a manger. Angels announce the birth to shepherds, who come and find the child. Forty days later his parents present him in the temple, where the aged Simeon and the prophetess Anna recognize him as God's salvation. At twelve, Jesus stays behind in the temple after Passover, and when his anxious parents find him among the teachers, he says he had to be in his Father's house.
story:
Chapter 1 announced two births and told the first; chapter 2 tells the greater one. Luke sets the birth of Jesus against the background of the Roman Empire, so that the emperor's decree moves a village couple to David's town, fulfilling a promise Augustus never heard of (Micah 5:2). The chapter then returns to the temple, where Luke's story began, and to faithful Israelites who were waiting for God's consolation. Simeon's words widen the horizon: this child is a light for the Gentiles as well as the glory of Israel, and he will cause the rise and fall of many. For the first time a shadow falls across the story, a sword that will pierce Mary's soul.

The birth of John in chapter 1 and the birth of Jesus here are told in matching steps (birth, circumcision and naming, a canticle, a note on the child's growth), and each time Jesus' story is fuller. John's birth is celebrated by neighbors; Jesus' by an army of angels. John grows up in the wilderness (1:80); Jesus grows up in Nazareth and is found in his Father's house. The chapter closes with the only story in the canonical Gospels from Jesus' childhood, in which his first recorded words speak of God as his Father, and then with about eighteen silent years in Nazareth before John appears in chapter 3.
historical:
Caesar Augustus, born Gaius Octavius and adopted as heir by his great-uncle Julius Caesar, became sole master of the Roman world after defeating Antony and Cleopatra at Actium in 31 BC, received the name Augustus in 27 BC, and ruled until his death in AD 14. His reign was celebrated as an age of peace; the Senate dedicated the Ara Pacis, the Altar of Augustan Peace, in Rome in 9 BC. In the same year the provincial assembly of Asia resolved to begin its calendar on his birthday, and the inscription recording the decision, best preserved at Priene, calls him a savior who ended war and says his birthday was the beginning of good news for the world (OGIS 458). Luke's angel announces a different Savior and different good news to shepherds in the fields.

Augustus did order censuses. His own record of his reign (Res Gestae 8) lists three counts of Roman citizens, in 28 BC, 8 BC, and AD 14, and provincial censuses for tribute were held in Gaul, Egypt, and elsewhere. Papyri from Roman Egypt show that households there registered every fourteen years, and an edict of the prefect Gaius Vibius Maximus in AD 104 ordered people living away from home to return to their districts for the census (P.London 904). The Roman jurist Ulpian (Digest 50.15.3) records that in Syria women as well as men were liable to the poll tax. What no source outside Luke describes is a Roman census in Herod's kingdom while he lived, since Judea was then a client kingdom, not a province.

The mention of Quirinius raises the best-known historical difficulty in the Gospels. Publius Sulpicius Quirinius, consul in 12 BC, became legate of Syria in AD 6, when Augustus deposed Herod's son Archelaus and Judea came under direct Roman rule; Josephus describes the census Quirinius then took in Judea (Antiquities 17.355, 18.1-2), which provoked the revolt of Judas the Galilean (Acts 5:37). A tombstone bought in Beirut in 1674 and now in Venice (the Lapis Venetus, ILS 2683) records a census he ordered at Apamea in Syria. But Luke 1:5 and Matthew 2:1 place Jesus' birth under Herod the Great, who died about 4 BC. The main solutions are set out in the first hard question below.

Bethlehem, about six miles south of Jerusalem, was David's hometown (1 Samuel 16-17), and Micah 5:2 had promised that a ruler of Israel would come from it. Justin Martyr, writing around AD 155, says Jesus was born in a cave near the village (Dialogue with Trypho 78); Origen (Against Celsus 1.51) says the cave and manger were being shown in his day; and Constantine built the Church of the Nativity over that cave in the 330s. Jerome later lived and translated the Bible in Bethlehem from 386 until his death. The temple courts where Simeon and Anna appear were part of Herod's rebuilt complex; the Mishnah places the purification of mothers after childbirth at the Nicanor Gate (m. Sotah 1:5).
cultural:
The word traditionally translated inn, kataluma, is the word Luke uses for the upper guest room of the Last Supper (22:11), while he uses a different word, pandocheion, for the Samaritan's inn (10:34). Kenneth Bailey (Jesus Through Middle Eastern Eyes, 2008) argued that Joseph and Mary stayed in a relative's village house whose guest room was full, and that the child was laid in a feeding trough in the main family room, where animals were brought in at night; Stephen Carlson (New Testament Studies, 2010) argued that kataluma simply means their place to stay, too cramped for a birth. Either reading replaces the picture of a heartless innkeeper, which the text never mentions. Swaddling cloths were strips of cloth wrapped snugly around a newborn, an ordinary act of care; Wisdom of Solomon 7:4-5 has Solomon say he was nursed in swaddling cloths, since no king has a different beginning.

Shepherds worked long hours outdoors and lived with their flocks, keeping watch in shifts through the night. David was a shepherd and God was Israel's shepherd (Psalm 23, Ezekiel 34), but the occupation carried little status, and later rabbinic sources list herding among trades that invite dishonesty (m. Qiddushin 4:14). How far those later texts reflect the first century is debated. The text gives no date for the birth; the December date is first clearly attested in the Roman Chronograph of 354.

The Law of Moses set out three rites that frame verses 21 to 24. A son was circumcised and named on the eighth day (Leviticus 12:3). A mother was ritually unclean for forty days after the birth of a son and then brought an offering for her purification: a lamb and a pigeon or dove, or, if she could not afford a lamb, two turtledoves or two young pigeons (Leviticus 12:6-8). Mary brings the poor family's offering. Every firstborn son belonged to God, because God spared Israel's firstborn at the Passover, and was redeemed with five shekels (Exodus 13:2, 13:12-15, Numbers 18:15-16); Luke mentions no payment and speaks instead of presenting the child, as Hannah presented Samuel (1 Samuel 1:22-28).

Faithful Jews went up to Jerusalem for the pilgrim festivals, Passover among them (Deuteronomy 16:16); the obligation fell on men, so Mary's going shows the family's devotion. Pilgrims from Galilee traveled in large groups of relatives and neighbors, the caravan Luke calls a sunodia, which explains how a twelve-year-old could be missed for a day. The Mishnah says a boy becomes obligated to the commandments at thirteen (m. Avot 5:21); the bar mitzvah ceremony is much later. Teachers of the Law held sessions in the temple courts, and a pupil sat among them, listening and asking questions, which is exactly Jesus' posture in verse 46.
literary:
The chapter is framed by the emperor's decree at the start and the temple at the center and end, and it falls into three scenes: the birth (verses 1 to 20), the presentation (verses 21 to 40), and the boy in the temple (verses 41 to 52). Each ends with a response: the shepherds glorify God, Simeon and Anna give thanks and speak of the child, and the teachers are astounded. Mary appears twice treasuring these things and pondering them in her heart (verses 19 and 51), a note many readers take as a hint that she was among the sources Luke's preface mentions. Two summary statements about Jesus' growth (verses 40 and 52) mirror the one about John (1:80) and echo the boy Samuel, who grew in stature and in favor with the Lord and with men (1 Samuel 2:26), completing a thread that runs from Hannah's song to Mary's.

Luke balances his cast. The emperor in Rome is set against a baby in a feeding trough; an army of angels against a few shepherds; the aged Simeon against the aged Anna, a man and a woman, as Luke often pairs them. The angels' announcement (verses 10 and 11) is the Gospel's first full proclamation, and its vocabulary (good news, Savior, today, peace) is the language of imperial propaganda claimed for another king. The angels' song (verse 14) and Simeon's (verses 29 to 32) are the third and fourth of Luke's canticles; Simeon's, called the Nunc Dimittis from its first words in Latin, draws on the servant songs of Isaiah (42:6, 49:6, 52:10), where God's servant is made a light for the nations.

The chapter moves steadily toward the temple and toward Jesus' own voice. In the first scene others speak about him; in the second he is carried into the temple and spoken over; in the third he speaks for himself, and his first words in the Gospel are two questions, the second of which names God as ‘My Father’. His parents do not understand, anticipating the disciples who will not understand his predictions of suffering (9:45, 18:34). The last verse is a summary that covers eighteen years in a sentence.

outline.t: The census and the birth in Bethlehem
The boy Jesus in the temple

doctrines.note: The Son of the Most High (1:32) is wrapped in cloths and laid in a feeding trough, and the sign by which the shepherds know him is his poverty (verse 12). He grows and becomes strong and increases in wisdom (verses 40 and 52), a real human childhood with real development. Athanasius answered the Arians that such growth belongs to the human nature the Word truly took, and the Chalcedonian confession of one person in two natures (451) gives this chapter room to mean what it says.

The angel announces a Savior who is Christ the Lord, born for all the people, and Simeon holds the child and says, “For my eyes have seen Your salvation.” Salvation in Luke is not first an idea but a person, and it arrives ‘today’ as good news of great joy, the word today that Luke will repeat at Nazareth (4:21), in Zacchaeus's house (19:9), and on the cross (23:43).

He is born in the city of David and called Christ the Lord, joining the royal title of the anointed king with the name kurios, which the Greek Old Testament uses for God. Simeon had been promised that he would see “the Lord’s Christ” before he died, and at twelve Jesus speaks of God as his own Father.

Jesus' parents do everything the Law of the Lord requires: circumcision on the eighth day, purification, presentation of the firstborn, and the yearly Passover. Luke cites the Law five times in the chapter (verses 22, 23, 24, 27, 39), showing the Savior born under the law and raised in faithful obedience within Israel's worship, as Paul says in Galatians 4:4.

Simeon calls Jesus “a light for revelation to the Gentiles, and for glory to Your people Israel.” From the first weeks of his life the salvation he brings is meant for the nations, and Luke's two volumes end with Paul in Rome announcing that this salvation has been sent to the Gentiles (Acts 28:28).

words.note: Sōtēr, savior, deliverer. It occurs twenty-four times in the New Testament, most often in the Pastoral Letters and 2 Peter; in the Gospels only here, in Mary's song (1:47, of God), and in John 4:42. The Greek Old Testament uses it of God, and the Roman world used it of gods, generals, and emperors, Augustus above all. The angel's announcement quietly sets two claims side by side: the emperor in Rome and the child in a manger.

Kataluma, a lodging place, guest room. It occurs three times in the New Testament: here and for the room of the Last Supper (Mark 14:14, Luke 22:11). Luke uses pandocheion for a commercial inn (10:34). The word supports the reading that there was no room in the guest room of the house where they stayed, not that an innkeeper turned them away, though the traditional rendering inn is still found in many translations.

Phatnē, manger, feeding trough, and by extension a stall. It occurs four times in the New Testament, three times in this chapter (verses 7, 12, 16) and once of the ox or donkey untied from the stall on the Sabbath (13:15). In the Greek of Isaiah 1:3 the ox knows its owner and the donkey its lord's manger while Israel does not know, the verse behind the ox and donkey of Christian art. The repeated word makes the feeding trough the sign by which the Savior is found.

Apographō, to register, enroll. It occurs four times in the New Testament, three here and once of the firstborn ‘enrolled in heaven’ (Hebrews 12:23); the noun apographē occurs in verse 2 and Acts 5:37. It describes an enrollment of persons and property, which could serve taxation but was not itself a tax. The same bureaucratic word that moves Joseph to Bethlehem later names the census that sparked Judas the Galilean's revolt.

Eudokia, good pleasure, favor, goodwill. It occurs nine times in the New Testament, usually of God's gracious will (Ephesians 1:5, 1:9). The angels' song blesses peace on earth to people of God's favor, the reading of the earliest manuscripts; later manuscripts read the nominative, which gives the familiar ‘goodwill toward men’. The Qumran Thanksgiving Hymns speak of the sons of his good pleasure for God's chosen. The peace is God's gift to those on whom his favor rests, not a general human mood.

Paraklēsis, encouragement, comfort, consolation. It occurs twenty-nine times in the New Testament, mostly in Paul, and twice in Luke's Gospel: Simeon is waiting for the consolation of Israel (verse 25), and the rich are warned that they have already received their comfort (6:24). The phrase draws on Isaiah 40:1, ‘Comfort, comfort My people’, where the Greek uses the related verb. Israel's consolation is the promised end of exile and the coming of God, and Simeon finds it in a child.

Sōtērion, saving, salvation (a neuter adjective used as a noun). It occurs four times in the New Testament: Simeon's ‘Your salvation’ (verse 30), the quotation of Isaiah 40:5 in Luke 3:6, Paul's last words in Acts 28:28, and the helmet of salvation in Ephesians 6:17. Three of the four are in Luke's writings, and they frame his two volumes: the salvation Simeon sees in the temple is the salvation Paul announces in Rome.

Dei, it is necessary, one must. It occurs about a hundred times in the New Testament, some forty of them in Luke and Acts, often for the necessity of God's plan. Jesus' first recorded words use it: “I had to be in My Father’s house.” The same word will mark his sense of divine purpose throughout Luke, from preaching the kingdom (4:43) to his suffering and rising (9:22, 24:7, 24:26). Even as a boy he knows he is under his Father's necessity.

christ:
Luke 2 shows the Son of God entering the world in poverty and obscurity. He is laid in a feeding trough, visited by shepherds, and presented in the temple with a poor family's offering, yet angels proclaim him Savior, Christ, and Lord. The three titles together say what the whole Gospel will unfold: he rescues, he is Israel's anointed king, and he bears the name that belongs to God. He is born in Bethlehem, the city of David, fulfilling Micah 5:2, which Matthew quotes (Matthew 2:6) and John's crowds recall (John 7:42), though Luke does not cite it.

In Simeon's words he is the salvation God has prepared in the sight of all people, the servant of Isaiah 49:6 who is a light for the nations. Malachi 3:1 had promised that the Lord would suddenly come to his temple; Luke shows him arriving as a forty-day-old infant carried by poor parents, recognized only by an old man and an old woman led by the Spirit. Simeon also speaks of a sign spoken against and a sword that will pierce Mary's soul, the first shadow of the cross in Luke. The stone imagery of Isaiah 8:14-15 and 28:16, which Jesus applies to himself in 20:17-18, stands behind the rise and fall of many.

At twelve Jesus calls God ‘My Father’ in a way his parents do not understand, and he knows he must be in his Father's house. Yet he goes home and is obedient to Joseph and Mary, and he grows in wisdom and stature, fully human in his development. The church confesses both truths together: he is truly God and truly man, who, as Paul says, emptied himself, taking the form of a servant (Philippians 2:7), and the Letter to the Hebrews says he was made like his brothers in every way (Hebrews 2:17). The one who will later give himself as the true Passover (22:15-20) is here a boy keeping the Passover with his family.
interpretation:
The birth story was retold and embellished early. The Protevangelium of James, from the second half of the second century, sets the birth in a cave outside Bethlehem, adds a midwife who confirms Mary's virginity, and supplied later art with many details. Justin Martyr (Dialogue with Trypho 78) knew the cave, and Justin (1 Apology 34) appealed to the census records under Quirinius as if they could be checked. Origen preached on the chapter at Caesarea, and his homilies on Simeon read the sword of verse 35 as the doubt that would pierce Mary at the cross. Athanasius (Against the Arians 3.51-53) used verse 52 to explain how the eternal Word could grow in wisdom according to his human nature. The Chronograph of 354 is the first clear witness to 25 December as the date of the birth, and Leo the Great's Christmas sermons in fifth-century Rome and Augustine's in Hippo made Luke 2 the church's Christmas text. The later Gospel of Pseudo-Matthew added the ox and the donkey from Isaiah 1:3, and Jerome, who lived in Bethlehem from 386, preached there on the manger.

Readers attentive to Jewish law have noted that Luke's account of the purification and presentation follows Leviticus 12 and Exodus 13 closely, though his ‘their purification’ in verse 22 does not match the law's wording; Raymond Brown took this as a sign that Luke was not intimately familiar with temple practice, while others read the plural as including Joseph or the family. Anna's portrait, a widow fasting in the temple into extreme old age, closely resembles the heroine of the book of Judith (Judith 8:4-6, 16:23).

In the Middle Ages the chapter shaped the church year and popular devotion. The Presentation was kept on 2 February, forty days after Christmas, as Candlemas in the West and as the Meeting (Hypapante) in the East, and the Nunc Dimittis was sung at Compline. According to Bonaventure's Life of Saint Francis, Francis of Assisi set up a manger with an ox and a donkey at Greccio at Christmas 1223, the root of the Christmas crib. Giotto's Nativity and Presentation in the Scrovegni Chapel in Padua (about 1305) gave the scenes lasting shape. The Reformers preached Luke 2 every Christmas; Luther's hymn Vom Himmel hoch (1535) turns the angel's message into a children's carol, and his Christmas sermons stress the lowliness of the birth.

The chapter is sung more than almost any other passage of Scripture. The Gloria in excelsis, which begins with verse 14, is attested in Greek by the fourth century and sung in the Western Mass. Bach's Christmas Oratorio (1734) sets Luke 2:1-21 in Luther's German, Handel's Messiah (1742) sets verses 8 to 14, and Rembrandt's last painting, left unfinished at his death in 1669, shows Simeon holding the child. William Holman Hunt's The Finding of the Saviour in the Temple (1854 to 1860) tried to paint verses 41 to 52 with archaeological accuracy. For many Americans the best-known reading is Linus's recital of verses 8 to 14 in the King James Version in A Charlie Brown Christmas (1965). In the lectionaries verses 1 to 14 (or 20) are the Gospel of the Christmas night Mass or first service of Christmas, and verses 22 to 40 are read at the Presentation.
text:
Several differences between English Bibles in this chapter come from the manuscripts. In verse 14 the Byzantine manuscripts read eudokia (nominative), which makes three phrases: glory to God, peace on earth, goodwill toward men, as in the King James Version. Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, Vaticanus (first hand), Bezae, and the Latin tradition read eudokias (genitive), ‘among people of his good pleasure’ or ‘on whom His favor rests’, which modern editions and translations follow. The difference is one letter, a final sigma easily lost in copying, and the Latin Vulgate's hominibus bonae voluntatis, ‘to men of good will’, reflects the genitive.

In verses 33 and 43 the earliest manuscripts read ‘his father and mother’ and ‘his parents’; the Byzantine text reads ‘Joseph and his mother’ in both places, as in the KJV, a change most scholars attribute to scribes protecting the virgin birth. In verse 22 the Greek manuscripts overwhelmingly read ‘their purification’, while a few late manuscripts followed by the Textus Receptus read ‘her purification’. In verse 5 the earliest manuscripts call Mary ‘betrothed’, while the Byzantine text adds ‘wife’ (the KJV's ‘espoused wife’). In verse 40 the Byzantine text adds ‘in spirit’, borrowed from 1:80. In verse 37 the earliest manuscripts read ‘until’ (heōs), which allows either a widow up to the age of eighty-four or a widow for eighty-four years, while the Byzantine text reads ‘about’ (hōs). In verse 2 no manuscript alters Quirinius's name or the word first; the difficulty there is historical, not textual.

teach.big: God keeps his promise by sending his Son into the world in poverty, announcing him to the lowly, and revealing him as the salvation of Israel and the light of the nations, a salvation that will also divide hearts and cost those who love him.

outline.t: God rules over the rulers: an emperor's decree brings David's heir to David's town, and the Son of God is born in the humblest conditions.
The good news comes first to the lowly, and the right responses to it are to go and see, to tell others, to praise God, and, like Mary, to ponder.
The Savior is born under the law and received into Israel through its ordinary rites by a poor and obedient family.
Simeon shows what patient hope looks like and sees that the child is salvation for all peoples, yet a sign that will be opposed and will expose hearts.
A long life of prayer and fasting prepares Anna to recognize the child and to speak of him to all who wait for redemption.
The Son of God grows up in an ordinary village under God's grace.
Jesus knows himself to be the Father's Son and yet lives in obedience to his earthly parents, growing in wisdom and favor.

teach.pitfalls:
Several misreadings are common at Christmas. The first is the cruel innkeeper, a character the text never mentions; the kataluma is more likely a guest room, and the point is humility, not rejection by a villain. The second treats the shepherds as outcasts on the basis of later rabbinic texts alone; Luke's readers would also think of David the shepherd king and the Lord as Israel's shepherd. The third is sentimentality: the manger is a sign of poverty, the angels are an army, and Simeon's blessing includes a sword. A Christmas sermon that omits verses 34 and 35 loses Luke's own shadow of the cross.

Avoid using verse 14 as a general blessing on human goodwill; the earliest text speaks of peace to those on whom God's favor rests. With the boy in the temple, avoid portraying Jesus as lecturing the teachers or as a disobedient child; he is listening and asking questions, and he goes home and is obedient. Avoid resolving the Quirinius question too quickly in either direction; it is a genuine historical puzzle, and honesty about it serves hearers better than confident overstatement.
teach.pastoral: This chapter speaks to the waiting. Simeon and Anna spent long years in prayer before they saw what they hoped for, and Anna's widowhood lasted decades; people who have lost a spouse or have waited long for God may find themselves in her. It also speaks to parents: Mary and Joseph lose their son for three days, search in anguish, and do not understand his answer. Parents of children who have wandered or who are hard to understand can see that even this family knew fear and misunderstanding. Simeon's warning to Mary acknowledges that love for Christ does not exempt anyone from grief.

hard.q: How can Luke date Jesus' birth to a census under Quirinius when Quirinius governed Syria in AD 6, about ten years after Herod the Great died?
hard.a:
The difficulty is real, and the strongest form of the objection has three parts. Josephus, our fullest source, describes Quirinius's census of Judea in AD 6, when Judea became a province, and says nothing of an earlier one. A Roman census in Herod's client kingdom would have been unusual, and no ancient source outside Luke mentions one. And registering in an ancestral town, rather than where one lived or held property, is not attested as Roman practice. Emil Schürer in his history of the Jewish people, Raymond Brown (The Birth of the Messiah, 1977), and Joseph Fitzmyer (Anchor Bible, 1981) concluded that Luke has confused the famous census of AD 6 with the time of Jesus' birth, and skeptical writers treat the passage as a clear historical error.

Several responses have been offered. The first is grammatical: Nigel Turner (1965) argued that the Greek word for first can mean before when followed by a genitive, giving ‘this census took place before Quirinius was governor of Syria’, distinguishing it from the famous one; most grammarians find this strained. The second proposes an earlier office for Quirinius. William Ramsay defended this, pointing to an anonymous career inscription from Tivoli (the Lapis Tiburtinus) that mentions a second term as legate of Syria, which Theodor Mommsen assigned to Quirinius; Ronald Syme and others assign it to another man, and Luke's verb for governing is general enough, some argue, to cover a special command. The third notes that Tertullian (Against Marcion 4.19) placed the census under Sentius Saturninus, governor about 9 to 6 BC, which may preserve an independent tradition, and that Justin Martyr (1 Apology 34) appealed to census records as if they could be checked. The fourth suggests that a registration begun under Herod, perhaps connected with the oath of loyalty to Augustus that Josephus says some six thousand Pharisees refused (Antiquities 17.42), was completed or became known under Quirinius. Defenders note that Luke elsewhere shows careful knowledge of Roman officials and titles, which is why scholars such as Darrell Bock and I. Howard Marshall give him the benefit of the doubt; critics reply that care elsewhere does not guarantee accuracy here. The question concerns a date. It does not touch the confession that Jesus was born in David's town as a real man in real history, and faithful Christians hold different views of how it should be resolved.

hard.q: Can Luke's account of Jesus' birth and childhood be reconciled with Matthew's?
hard.a:
The objection is that the two stories seem to describe different families. In Matthew, Joseph and Mary apparently live in Bethlehem, where the magi find the child in a house (Matthew 2:11); the family flees to Egypt to escape Herod's massacre and settles in Nazareth only afterward, to avoid Archelaus. In Luke, they live in Nazareth, travel to Bethlehem for the census, present the child in the temple forty days later, and return peacefully to Nazareth (verse 39), with no magi, no massacre, and no Egypt. Matthew's story is told from Joseph's side, with dreams; Luke's from Mary's, with angels and songs. David Friedrich Strauss (1835) and, more recently, Geza Vermes (The Nativity: History and Legend, 2006) and Marcus Borg and John Dominic Crossan (The First Christmas, 2007) concluded that the two accounts are independent theological compositions that cannot both be history.

Others note how much the two accounts share while writing independently. Raymond Brown listed their common points: Mary a virgin betrothed to Joseph, conception by the Holy Spirit, an angel's announcement, the name Jesus given from heaven, Joseph of David's line, birth in Bethlehem in the days of Herod, and upbringing in Nazareth. Harmonizers such as Craig Blomberg (The Historical Reliability of the Gospels, 1987) and Darrell Bock suggest a sequence: birth in Bethlehem, presentation in Jerusalem, a stay in Bethlehem long enough for the magi to find the family in a house (Herod kills boys up to two years old), the flight to Egypt, and the return to Nazareth, with Luke's verse 39 compressing the interval and Matthew omitting the earlier home in Nazareth. Critics answer that this reads each Gospel against its natural sense. Moderate scholars often conclude that both evangelists drew on genuine traditions about Jesus' origins and shaped them for their own purposes. How far the accounts can be fitted together is a question on which scholars who share a high view of Scripture still differ.

observe: What titles does the angel give the newborn child in verse 11, and what sign does he give the shepherds in verse 12?
Count how many times the chapter mentions the Law of the Lord. What do Joseph and Mary do to keep it?
What does Simeon say about the child to God (verses 29-32), and what does he say to Mary (verses 34-35)?
interpret: Why might Luke set the birth of Jesus against the decree of Caesar Augustus, whom the empire called savior and bringer of good news?
What does Simeon mean by calling Jesus both a light for the Gentiles and a sign that will be spoken against?
How can Jesus know he must be in his Father's house and still go home and be obedient to his parents? What does verse 52 say about his humanity?
apply: The birth of the Savior was announced first to shepherds, not to rulers or priests. Whose voice might God be using in your life that you would be tempted to overlook?
Simeon and Anna waited for years in prayer and worship before they saw what they hoped for. What helps you keep hoping when God's promises seem slow?
Mary treasured and pondered what she did not yet understand. What experience of God in your life are you still pondering?
